identification.summary: admin@338 is a China-based cyber espionage group. FireEye says it has used newsworthy events as lures and has mostly targeted organizations involved in financial, economic and trade policy, usually with publicly available RATs such as Poison Ivy plus some non-public backdoors [S1][S6]. The name comes from a password the operators used with Poison Ivy [S3]. In March 2014 the group sent spear-phishing lures themed on Malaysian Airlines MH370 to an Asia-Pacific government and a US-based think tank [S4][S5]. In August 2015 FireEye linked it, with hedging, to spear phishing against Hong Kong media using the Dropbox-abusing LOWBALL backdoor [S1].
identification.firstObserved: Coverage of FireEye's 2013 Poison Ivy report says the group used Poison Ivy from about January 2008 [S3]. FireEye's 2015 post says FireEye had tracked the group since 2013 [S1][S7].
identification.notes: FireEye treated admin@338 as an uncategorized APT group with no APT number, saying it lacked enough information to assign one [S1]. MITRE tracks the group as admin@338 (G0018) [S6]. MISP-derived aliases TEMPER PANDA (CrowdStrike), Team338 and MAGNESIUM are already on the record. None of the sources opened for this profile give a current Microsoft Typhoon name for MAGNESIUM. Some low-quality secondary blogs equate admin@338 with APT18, Dynamite Panda, TigerMilk or Poseidon Group. Those are separately tracked clusters, and no primary source reviewed supports the merge, so they are not added.

attribution.sponsor: Not formally attributed by any government in the sources reviewed. FireEye describes the group as China-based [S1][S4].
attribution.confidence: FireEye said only that admin@338 'may have conducted' the 2015 Hong Kong media activity. It explicitly declined to attribute a second, related Dropbox-based operation to the group [S1]. The China-based assessment comes from FireEye, not from a government [S1].
attribution.basis: FireEye malware and infrastructure analysis. A BUBBLEWRAP sample in the 2015 campaign connected to a domain that resolved to an IP address the group had used before [S1]. Poison Ivy connection passwords linked the 2014 MH370 lures to the group [S4][S5]. FireEye also judged that the targets matched Beijing's likely intelligence interests [S1].

objectives: Espionage. Earlier collection focused on financial, economic and trade-policy information [S1][S2]. FireEye assessed that the 2015 targeting of Hong Kong media was probably a response to political and economic challenges in Hong Kong and China. It said that access could give the government advance warning of protests, information on pro-democracy leaders, and insight needed to disrupt activity on the Internet [S1].

sectors: Financial services and financial, economic and trade-policy organizations [S1][S2]
ISP/telecommunications, government and defense (secondary per FireEye 2013) [S3]
targeting.notes: FireEye noted that the August 2015 campaign was the first it had seen from this group aimed at readers of traditional Chinese script. Earlier lures were in English and aimed at Western audiences [S1]. The campaign coincided with criminal charges against democracy activists and followed the late-2014 Umbrella Movement protests [S1].

capabilities.summary: Spear phishing with topical, news-cycle lure documents [S1][S4]. These included Word documents exploiting the old Office vulnerability CVE-2012-0158 [S1] and an executable disguised as a Flash video by binding a Flash icon to it [S4]. Malware includes the Poison Ivy RAT [S2][S4], WinHTTPHelper [S5], and the first-stage LOWBALL backdoor. LOWBALL uses the Dropbox API with a hard-coded bearer token over HTTPS port 443 for command and control, and runs operator-supplied batch files to gather directory, network, user/group, service and netstat information [S1]. The second-stage BUBBLEWRAP backdoor (Backdoor.APT.FakeWinHTTPHelper) persists at boot, communicates over HTTP, HTTPS or SOCKS, and supports plugins [S1]. Dropbox revoked the access token LOWBALL used after FireEye notified it [S1][S7].

campaigns.name: Poison Ivy espionage against finance and policy targets
campaigns.summary: In its 2013 Poison Ivy report, FireEye identified admin@338 as one of three groups (with th3bug and menuPass) using Poison Ivy in targeted attacks. It said admin@338 mainly targeted financial services, with significant activity against the ISP/telecom, government and defense sectors [S2][S3].

campaigns.name: MH370-themed spear phishing
campaigns.summary: On 10 March 2014, two days after the flight disappeared, the group sent a 'Malaysian Airlines MH370.doc' lure that dropped Poison Ivy to a government in the Asia-Pacific region. On 14 March it sent MH370-themed lures to a US-based think tank [S4][S5].

campaigns.name: Hong Kong media spear phishing (LOWBALL / Dropbox C2)
campaigns.summary: Traditional-Chinese lures about an Umbrella Movement anniversary and a Hong Kong University referendum carried CVE-2012-0158 Word exploits. They targeted Hong Kong newspapers, radio and TV, delivering LOWBALL with Dropbox command and control and the BUBBLEWRAP second stage. FireEye said admin@338 'may have' conducted the activity. It also found a possibly related second operation with up to 50 targets that it did not attribute [S1][S7].

diamond.adversary: China-based espionage group that FireEye tracks as an uncategorized APT. No government attribution has been made [S1].
diamond.capability: Topical spear-phishing lures, CVE-2012-0158 Office exploits, Poison Ivy, WinHTTPHelper, LOWBALL and BUBBLEWRAP [S1][S4][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Legitimate cloud storage (a Dropbox account and API token) used as command and control. Dynamic-DNS-style domains such as accounts.serveftp[.]com resolving to IPs the group had used before [S1].
diamond.victim: Financial, economic and trade-policy organizations; Asia-Pacific government officials; a US think tank; Hong Kong media [S1][S2][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection aligned with Beijing's interest in economic policy and, per FireEye, in monitoring Hong Kong's pro-democracy movement and the press that covers it [S1].
diamond.technology: Unpatched Microsoft Office (CVE-2012-0158), user trust in news-related attachments, and trusted cloud services that mix C2 traffic into normal HTTPS [S1][S4].

gaps: No admin@338 activity after 2015 was found in the sources reviewed. Whether the group is still active, has been renamed or has been merged into another vendor cluster is unknown.
Microsoft's current name for MAGNESIUM, if any, was not confirmed. No Microsoft source was found.

The primary FireEye 2013 reports ('Poison Ivy: Assessing Damage and Extracting Intelligence' and 'Know Your Enemy: Tracking a Rapidly Evolving APT Actor') could not be opened. Their content here relies on press coverage [S2][S3].
The FireEye MH370 blog was seen only through a mirror and coverage. The MITRE ATT&CK, CFR Cyber Operations Tracker, Security Affairs and Dark Reading pages could not be fetched (DNS failures).
FireEye's attribution of the 2015 campaign is hedged ('may have'). The second Dropbox operation (up to 50 targets) is explicitly unattributed [S1].
Secondary blogs claim links to APT18, Dynamite Panda, TigerMilk, Poseidon Group and the MSS. None of these is supported by a primary source reviewed, so they are excluded.
Claims of a separate 2014 theft of classified MH370 investigation documents were not tied to admin@338 by any source reviewed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): User email clients and Office document handling are key terrain, as are outbound HTTPS channels to sanctioned cloud storage, which this actor used for command and control [S1]. STEP 2 (effects): News-cycle lures (MH370, protests, political events) reach targets within days of an event, so lure risk rises during any high-profile crisis involving US or allied forces [S1][S4]. STEP 3 (adversary model): Topical spear phish, then an Office exploit or disguised executable, then a first-stage backdoor running discovery commands (directory, ipconfig, net user/group, services, netstat), then a second-stage persistent backdoor [S1]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is email-borne collection against policy, finance and think-tank-adjacent staff using topical lures and cloud-storage C2. MDCOA is persistent, low-visibility access to planning or liaison networks through trusted-cloud C2 that blends with normal traffic. Candidate indicators: Office documents exploiting CVE-2012-0158; executables with Flash icons; Dropbox API calls from non-browser processes with bearer tokens; files named [COMPUTER_NAME]_upload.bat or _download; connections to accounts.serveftp[.]com [S1][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: Track news-event lure activity and cloud-service API use from unusual processes. FireEye's case shows that defender-provider coordination (Dropbox revoking the token) can sever C2 [S1]. Authorities: Disrupting actor use of a commercial cloud account depends on the provider and on law-enforcement or industry channels, not DoD action. Mission assurance: Patch legacy Office vulnerabilities and restrict executable attachments, because the documented access vectors are old exploits and disguised executables [S1][S4]. Coordination: Share indicators with cloud providers, and with partners whose staff (think tanks, policy and finance liaisons) were historically targeted [S1][S4].

provenance.importedSummary: China-based cyber threat group. It has previously used newsworthy events as lures to deliver malware and has primarily targeted organizations involved in financial, economic, and trade policy, typically using publicly available RATs such as PoisonIvy, as well as some non-public backdoors. This threat actor targets prodemocratic activists and organizations in Hong Kong, European and international financial institutions, and a U.S.-based think tank.
